paper_title: From Short Clips to Real-Time Streams: Identity-Aware Supervision and Context-Efficient Generation for Video Face Swapping

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Video face swapping transfers the reference identity to a target video while preserving its other attributes and motion. Despite recent progress in reference-guided flow-based methods, jointly achieving faithful identity transfer, high fidelity, and real-time generation over long video streams remains challenging. To address this challenge, we rethink the task-specific structure of reference-guided video face swapping. First, face swapping changes only identity while preserving most visual content, yet flow-matching supervision is weakly sensitive to these changes. We therefore develop Joint Rec-ID Loss, which balances explicit identity supervision and latent reconstruction according to the noise level. Second, the target video already provides non-edited attributes and temporal dynamics, enabling generation with fewer spatial tokens and shorter temporal contexts through Face-RoI Generation and Short-Context Rollout Training. By integrating these designs, we propose StreamingSwap, a reference-guided flow-matching framework for real-time streaming video face swapping. We also introduce HumanFaceVid, comprising 1,000 hours of cinematic training data and evaluation sets of 200 short and 200 long videos. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves competitive identity transfer and visual quality at 20 FPS on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, with stable generation over videos up to 10 minutes long. Project webpage: https://aim-uofa.github.io/StreamingSwap/

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Video face swapping transfers identity from source image to target video while preserving other target attributes, such as expression, pose, gaze, illumination, and background. It has broad applications in film production, AI-generated dramas, and live streaming. GAN-based approaches (Chen et al., 2020; Shiohara et al., 2023; Luo et al., 2025; Henry, 2025) offer strong identity transfer and efficient inference, but processing frames independently can introduce visual artifacts and temporal flicker. To improve realism and temporal coherence, diffusion-based approaches leverage the generative priors of pretrained video diffusion models. Among these, inpainting-based approaches (Han et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024; Shao et al., 2024) mask the target face and reconstruct it conditioned on source identity and auxiliary attributes, but removing direct access to fine-grained target cues makes non-edited attributes difficult to preserve faithfully. Recent reference-guided methods, represented by LivingSwap (Luo et al., 2026) and DreamIDV (Guo et al., 2026), construct paired supervision to retain the complete target video as visual reference, enabling more faithful preservation of fine-grained target attributes. However, the unmasked target face contains not only the attributes to be preserved but also the identity to be replaced, creating competing identity signal that makes source-identity injection difficult. Meanwhile, these methods are fine-tuned from large-scale video diffusion models (Wan et al., 2025) and remain computationally expensive due to iterative full-frame denoising over long temporal contexts. Consequently, extending their high-fidelity results to real-time, long-duration generation while ensuring faithful source-identity transfer remains difficult. These challenges motivate us to rethink reference-guided video face swapping through its taskspecific structure. First, video face swapping changes only identity while preserving most visual content in the target video. This leaves flow-matching supervision with weak signal for identity transfer, as identity differences account for only small fraction of the latent reconstruction error. Second, the target video directly provides the non-edited attributes and temporal dynamics to be preserved. Yet existing reference-guided methods still process background over long temporal contexts, resulting in substantial computational redundancy. Guided by these observations, we introduce STREAMINGSWAP, the first reference-guided flowmatching framework for real-time, long-duration video face swapping. To strengthen source-identity transfer, Joint Rec-ID Loss combines clean-latent reconstruction with explicit identity supervision, balancing their relative contributions according to the noise level. For efficient generation, Face-RoI Generation restricts video conditioning and generation to face-region tokens, avoiding redundant background computation. To enable streaming, Short-Context Rollout Training trains the bidirectional model through autoregressive rollout with short generated history, reducing the mismatch between training and inference while retaining bidirectional generation within each window. We further introduce HumanFaceVid, cinematic video face-swapping dataset constructed from OpenHumanVid (Li et al., 2025), comprising 1,000 hours of training data and evaluation sets of 200 short and 200 long videos. Across diverse scenarios, STREAMINGSWAP improves identity similarity while preserving target attributes and maintaining high video quality. It processes videos at 20 FPS on single NVIDIA 4090 GPU and maintains stable generation for videos up to 10 minutes. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We identify and examine two task-specific properties of reference-guided video face swapping: latent flow-matching supervision is weakly sensitive to identity changes, while target-provided visual information allows generation with fewer spatial tokens and shorter temporal contexts. We introduce STREAMINGSWAP, which combines Joint Rec-ID Loss, Face-RoI Generation, and Short-Context Rollout Training to enable real-time streaming video face swapping. It achieves 20 FPS on single NVIDIA 4090 GPU with stable generation on videos up to 10 minutes long. We construct HumanFaceVid, comprising 1,000 hours of cinematic training data derived from OpenHumanVid and evaluation sets of 200 short and 200 long videos for assessing identity fidelity, target-attribute preservation, visual quality, and temporal stability.

sections.title: 3 TASK-SPECIFIC ANALYSIS
sections.content: The difficulty of combining faithful identity transfer, high visual quality, and real-time long-video generation motivates us to revisit video face swapping through its task-specific structure. Compared with general-purpose video editing, reference-guided face swapping has two distinctive properties. First, face swapping has restricted editing scope: only facial identity should change, while all other facial attributes and content outside the face region should remain consistent with the target video. However, the flow matching objective optimizes reconstruction loss over the latent representation of the entire image, which may be insufficiently sensitive to identity changes when most visual content remains unchanged. To quantify this potential mismatch, we investigate how strongly the flow-matching objective penalizes identity-transfer failures (Q1). Second, the desired output is densely specified by visual inputs: the source image provides the identity, while the target video supplies not only non-identity facial attributes within the edited region but also the surrounding content and temporal dynamics. Nevertheless, existing reference-guided methods generate full frames, including regions that require no editing, and attend over extended temporal contexts to maintain consistency. To examine this potential computational redundancy, we investigate how much spatial and temporal context is actually required to preserve fidelity (Q2). We investigate these questions through two controlled analysis experiments. 3.1 IDENTITY SENSITIVITY OF FLOW-MATCHING SUPERVISION Setup. Under the linear probability path in Eq. 1, the predicted velocity determines the clean-latent estimate ˆx1 = xt + σtvθ(xt, cswap, t). Under role-reversed training, model that ignores Ir and reconstructs the target video Vg is penalized according to the latent distance between Vg and the ground-truth video Vr. This latent distance therefore provides diagnostic of the flow-matching supervision sensitivity to identity differences. We randomly sample 64 real videos Vr. For each video, we select five identity images {I (k) k=1 with varying identity similarities to Ir, including Ir as the self-swap control. Following the paireddata construction used for training, we use InSwapper (Henry, 2025) to generate (k) , Vr). We encode Vr and each (k) using Eϕ to compute their face-region latent MSE following Eq. 7, and measure identity similarity between the two videos. To contextualize the MSE scale, the qualitative visualization additionally includes mildly blurred identity-preserving version of Vr as reference. = S(I (k) }5 Results. As shown in Fig. 2(a), identity similarity changes by more than 0.75 across the constructed pairs, whereas mean face-region latent MSE varies by less than 0.05. The identity-preserving selfswap (third column) and mild-blur controls (second column) contextualize this error scale: visually minor deviations already produce latent MSEs around 0.15, comparable to or larger than those caused by visible identity changes (last column). This mismatch is consistent with the observation that swapping identity leaves most facial content, including expression, pose, and illumination, largely unchanged. At fixed noise level, the corresponding flow-matching penalty therefore changes little as the identity discrepancy increases. These results suggest that flow-matching supervision can support identity transfer but provides only weak signal for identity changes. 3.2 SPATIAL AND TEMPORAL CONTEXT REQUIREMENTS Setup. We examine the spatial and temporal context required by DreamID-V (Guo et al., 2026) using the same 64 evaluation cases. We independently vary the spatial coverage and temporal attention range of the video tokens Hvid R(hwF )d defined in Eq. 3. Spatially, we restrict token selection along the spatial grid while retaining all temporal frames. We progressively narrow the retained spatial region from the full frame to an enlarged face editing region. For the retained video-token indices Jρ, the selected token sequence and its spatial coverage are given by (ρ) vid = Hvid[Jρ], ρ = Jρ hwF , (8) where ρ = 100% corresponds to full-frame processing. Temporally, we use an attention mask to restrict each video tokens temporal context to neighboring latent frames. We vary over {20, 14, 10, 6, 4, 2}, with = 20 = 1 corresponding to full temporal bidirectional attention. We report identity similarity, expression and lighting errors, imaging quality, generation throughput in FPS, and computational cost in TFLOPs. For visualization, Fig. 2 aggregates expression error, lighting error, and imaging quality into normalized fidelity-and-quality score. Results. Spatially, Fig. 2(b) shows that reducing the retained-token ratio from 100% to 39% largely preserves identity similarity and the fidelity-and-quality score, while increasing generation throughput from approximately 1.3 to 2.2 FPS and reducing computation from 8,900 to 2,200 TFLOPs. This result indicates that background tokens contribute substantial computation but limited information once the target face region is available in reference-guided methods. Temporally, Fig. 2(c) shows that reducing the visible context from full attention to six neighboring latent frames causes only moderate quality degradation while increasing generation throughput and reducing computational cost. Performance drops sharply with fewer neighboring frames, particularly at = 2. These results suggest that short temporal context is sufficient for reference-guided generation, as the target video already provides the content and motion cues needed for long-range consistency. The temporal context therefore serves primarily to maintain local continuity. Summary. Together, the two experiments motivate the following design principles: 5 Figure 3: Overview of STREAMINGSWAP. Phase restricts video processing to face-RoI tokens and balances latent reconstruction with identity supervision through noise-dependent weighting. Phase II fine-tunes the model through self-rollout with short generated histories, enabling streaming inference while retaining bidirectional generation within each chunk. Explicit identity supervision. Training should directly supervise source identity to complement the weak sensitivity of latent reconstruction to identity changes. Focused spatial and temporal computation. Generation should exploit the target-provided content and motion to concentrate computation on face-region tokens and short temporal context.

sections.title: 4 METHOD
sections.content: 4.1 OVERVIEW Our pipeline comprises data preparation, two training phases, and streaming inference. We first construct the reversed pairs as in App. B. Phase adapts reference-guided video flow model with Joint Rec-ID Loss and Face-RoI Generation. Phase II employs Short-Context Rollout Training, exposing the model to its own generated short history for autoregressive long-video inference  (Fig. 3)  . 4.2 PHASE I: IDENTITY-AWARE FACE-ROI TRAINING We adopt the architecture and reference-guided training setup described in Sec. 2.2, initializing the model with pretrained DreamID-V weights (Guo et al., 2026). Guided by our task-specific analysis, we introduce two modifications. Face-RoI Generation. The analysis in Sec. 3.2 suggests that processing background tokens incurs substantial computational cost while providing limited performance gains. We therefore restrict spatial token coverage to an enlarged face region. Specifically, we downsample the binary face masks to the latent grid using max pooling and spatially dilate the resulting masks to define the compute region. We select all patches intersecting this region, denoting their token indices by Jroi and the latent positions they cover by Ωroi. As illustrated in Fig. 3 (left), the Transformer input is Hroi = Concatseq [Hid, Hvid[Jroi]] . (9) Selected video tokens retain their original spatiotemporal positional encodings. To support batched training, we pad sequences to the maximum length within each batch and mask out padding tokens in attention. We recover the clean RoI latent estimate ˆx1,roi from the predicted velocity following Eq. 6. This estimate is scattered back to the full latent grid and blended with the target-video latent xg = Eϕ(Vg): x1 = Mblend ScatterΩroi (ˆx1,roi) + (1 Mblend) xg, (10) where ScatterΩroi restores the predicted latents to their original positions. The feathered blending mask Mblend is derived from the same downsampled face masks, with weights transitioning smoothly from 1 in the inner face region to 0 outside the compute region. 6 Joint Rec-ID Loss. Our analysis in Sec. 3.2 motivates simpler adaptation for reference-guided face swapping: the target video supplies content and motion cues, so short generated history can provide context for local temporal continuity. We therefore retain bidirectional attention within each window and condition the generation of new frames on this short history. The condition c(n) swap includes the source image and aligned target-video and mask inputs covering both the history and new frames. History latents remain fixed at σ = 0 throughout denoising. The predicted RoI latents are composited using Eq. 10, and the latest composited frames provide history for the next window. The first window generates Nctx + Ngen latent frames without history. We use Nctx = 3 and Ngen = 9 to balance generation quality, throughput, and latency (App. G). Training with ground-truth history creates mismatch with streaming inference, where prediction errors can propagate through the generated history and accumulate across chunks. Inspired by Self Forcing (Huang et al., 2025), we fine-tune the Phase-I model through autoregressive self-rollout, exposing it to its own generated history during training (Fig. 3, right). We use 4-step denoising schedule, as the Phase-I model achieves comparable identity and target-attribute performance with 4 and 25 steps at substantially higher throughput (App. E). Following the stochastic gradienttruncation strategy of Self Forcing, we randomly select denoising step as the stopping point and backpropagate only through the clean-latent prediction at that step. Gradients are stopped through both the generated history and preceding denoising steps. sections.title: 5 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We initialize STREAMINGSWAP from DreamID-V (Guo et al., 2026) and train each phase for 1,000 iterations. We evaluate identity similarity, target-attribute preservation, FVD, and end-to-end inference efficiency. All speed measurements use single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. Detailed metrics and implementation settings are provided in App. D. 5.1 COMPARISONS WITH EXISTING METHODS We compare STREAMINGSWAP with two representative GAN-based methods and four diffusionbased methods that can run on single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, with quantitative and qualitative results in Table 1 and Fig. 4. Long-video comparisons include three strong-performing methods. Across both benchmarks, STREAMINGSWAP achieves effective identity transfer while preserving target fidelity and visual realism. Although InSwapper and DreamID-V achieve higher identity similarity, the frame-level scores in Fig. 4 illustrate that higher embedding similarity does not necessarily 8 Table 2: Ablation of the main components. DreamID-V exhibits pronounced changes in lighting and head pose despite high ID Sim. scores, while InSwappers high scores coexist with less realism in the displayed examples. In contrast, STREAMINGSWAP maintains recognizable source identity while more closely following the target lighting, expressions, and head poses. These comparisons highlight the importance of balancing identity similarity and target-attribute reconstruction, as further examined in App. F. Overall, STREAMINGSWAP offers balanced qualityefficiency, exceeding 20 FPS and achieving substantially higher throughput than the evaluated diffusion baselines. 5.2 ABLATION OF IDENTITY-AWARE SUPERVISION AND EFFICIENT CONTEXT Setup. We separately remove identity supervision and Face-RoI in Phase I, evaluating all variants with 25 denoising steps. For Phase II, we replace self-rollout with ground-truth-history conditioning and evaluate both variants using four-step inference. Table 2 and Fig. 5 summarize the results. Identity supervision. Removing identity supervision weakens source-identity transfer despite improving target-attribute scores, as also reflected in the visual examples. This confirms the analysis in Sec. 3.1: flow matching supervision alone is insufficient to ensure the intended identity edit. Face-RoI processing. Face-RoI substantially increases throughput while maintaining comparable identity and target-attribute scores. This is consistent with the analysis in Sec. 3.2: background tokens add substantial computation but little useful information. Self-rollout training. The results in Fig. 5 suggest that self-rollout training mitigates error accumulation across streaming windows by exposing the model to its own generated history.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented STREAMINGSWAP, reference-guided framework for streaming video face swapping that aligns supervision and computation with the task requirements. Our analysis motivates 9 Joint Rec-ID Loss to strengthen identity transfer, alongside Face-RoI Generation and Short-Context Rollout Training to reduce spatial and temporal computation. We also introduced HumanFaceVid to support training and evaluation on short and long videos. Experiments demonstrate competitive identity transfer and target fidelity at over 20 FPS on single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, with stable generation on videos up to 10 minutes long. These results show that task-specific supervision and compact context can make reference-guided generation substantially more efficient.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: We used Codex to assist with ChineseEnglish translation, language refinement, interpretation of experimental results, and figure and table organization and LaTeX formatting. We also used pretrained face-swapping model to construct synthetic training videos, as described in Appendix B. The synthetic data were filtered using identity similarity and other quality metrics, followed by manual inspection of randomly sampled examples. The authors take responsibility for the final content of this work, including all AI-assisted text.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: This work develops video face-swapping techniques for research and creative applications, including film production, AI-generated dramas, and live streaming. We recognize that realistic identity manipulation can be misused for impersonation, misinformation, and non-consensual content creation, and that efficient streaming may increase these risks. The additional application demos use video clips obtained from Bilibili and reference images located through Google Images. The faceswapped outputs are synthetic research demonstrations and should not be interpreted as authentic recordings or endorsements by the depicted individuals. We oppose deceptive and non-consensual uses of this technology and advocate obtaining appropriate permissions and consent, respecting privacy and content ownership, and clearly labeling manipulated media. REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT The method section describes Face-RoI processing, joint reconstructionidentity supervision, shortcontext rollout training, and streaming inference. Appendix details the data preparation pipeline. Appendix provides additional training and evaluation settings, including model initialization, hyperparameters, sampling and window configurations, metric definitions, and hardware and acceleration settings. We also specify the timing scope for end-to-end efficiency measurements. Together, these descriptions support reproduction of the method and its experimental evaluation.

sections.title: A RELATED WORK
sections.content: Video face swapping transfers the identity of source face to target video while preserving targetspecific attributes such as expression, pose, illumination, motion, and background. Existing approaches can be broadly grouped into GAN-based methods, which emphasize efficient feed-forward synthesis, and diffusion-based methods, which leverage generative priors to improve visual quality and temporal coherence. A.1 GAN-BASED VIDEO FACE SWAPPING GAN-based face swapping learns efficient feed-forward generators under adversarial supervision (Goodfellow et al., 2014). Early systems used shared encoders with identity-specific decoders and therefore required separate training for each identity pair (DeepFakes, 2020). Later subjectagnostic methods inject source-identity features into target representations and improve identity transfer or identity-attribute disentanglement through specialized architectures, objectives, and identity encoders (Li et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2020; Shiohara et al., 2023). CanonSwap extends this direction to videos by modifying identity in canonical space before restoring target motion (Luo et al., 2025). InSwapper is widely used one-shot model distributed through the InsightFace ecosystem, although its architecture and training procedure are not publicly documented Henry (2025). While these methods offer efficient inference, most image-based variants process videos frame by frame and thus do not explicitly model temporal dependencies. A.2 DIFFUSION-BASED VIDEO FACE SWAPPING The rapid development and application of diffusion models (Ho et al., 2020; Rombach et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025; 2026) have enabled second line of face-swapping methods with stronger generative priors. One branch follows an inpainting-oriented formulation, in which the target face is masked or otherwise reconstructed from the source identity and explicit targetattribute conditions. DiffSwap formulates face swapping as conditional inpainting and combines masked diffusion with identity and 3D facial guidance (Zhao et al., 2023). Face-Adapter introduces lightweight modules for injecting source identity, spatial structure, and detailed target attributes into pretrained image diffusion models (Han et al., 2024). Extending this formulation to videos, DynamicFace decomposes facial conditions using 3D priors and incorporates temporal modeling, while HiFiVFS builds on pretrained video diffusion model with disentangled target-attribute extraction and detailed identity injection (Wang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024). VividFace jointly trains on images and videos and introduces video-oriented VAE, identity-attribute disentanglement data, and 3D facial guidance to improve temporal consistency and robustness (Shao et al., 2024). Related identity-control frameworks instead introduce lightweight conditional branches into pretrained video generators and can be adapted to face swapping, although face swapping is not their primary formulation Xue et al. (2026). These approaches improve synthesis quality and temporal modeling, but reconstructing removed target face from auxiliary conditions can discard fine-grained appearance cues that are difficult to recover explicitly. more recent reference-guided branch retains the complete target video as visual condition and learns face swapping from synthetically constructed pairs. LivingSwap reverses GAN-generated training pairs so that real videos provide reconstruction targets, and uses edited keyframes together with temporal stitching to maintain identity across video chunks (Luo et al., 2026). DreamID-V constructs bidirectional identity supervision through SyncID-Pipe and trains Diffusion Transformer with modality-aware conditioning, curriculum learning, and identity-coherence optimization (Guo et al., 2026). By directly observing the target face, reference-guided models can preserve finegrained expressions, illumination, makeup, and occlusions more faithfully. However, access to the complete target face also allows the model to reconstruct most of the video while responding weakly to the source identity, and existing systems retain the computational cost of full-frame, chunk-based diffusion generation. Our work follows the reference-guided formulation but studies different boundary: identity-sensitive supervision and efficient streaming inference using face-region generation and fixed-size generated history. 13 Figure 6: Data preparation and role-reversed training for HumanFaceVid. We extract face-centered clips Vr and aligned masks , and select source image Ir with the same identity. InSwapper transfers another identity to Vr, followed by facial-contour warping to construct the pseudo-input Vg. sections.title: B DATA PREPARATION
sections.content: We construct HumanFaceVid from OpenHumanVid (Li et al., 2025). We detect and track faces, discard short or unreliable tracks, and obtain frame-aligned binary face masks by combining BiSeNet face parsing (Yu et al., 2018) with InsightFace landmark convex hulls (InsightFace). Source images are selected from cross-video identity clusters, yielding real imagevideo pairs (Ir, Vr) of the same identity. For each real video, face-swapping model InSwapper (Henry, 2025) transfers different identity to produce the generated video Vg in Eq. 5. We additionally apply temporally smoothed random facial-contour warps to Vg, guided by MediaPipe landmarks (Google), to reduce residual geometric identity cues. The resulting data are used in the reversed formulation, with the original real video retained as ground-truth supervision.

sections.title: C APPLICATIONS IN DIFFERENT SCENARIOS
sections.content: Figures 79 illustrate applications of STREAMINGSWAP to movies, live and online videos, and AI-generated short dramas. Movie footage requires identity editing to preserve both cinematic lighting and the nuances of the original performance. The displayed results follow the target videos illumination, subtle facial expressions, and head poses, including shots with partial occlusion, integrating the source identity while retaining the scenes visual character. Live and online videos require sustained streaming generation that follows speakers expressions and head movements. Our method supports continuous processing with stable facial appearance in the displayed sequences, including partially occluded faces. Its streaming throughput makes it suitable for live-video applications whose frame-rate and buffering requirements match the measured processing speed and latency. AI-generated short dramas present another use case: reinforcing character identity when large motions, complex lighting, or exaggerated expressions cause identity drift. By applying consistent source identity to the generated footage, STREAMINGSWAP provides an efficient post-processing step that strengthens identity consistency while retaining the original performance and scene context, without regenerating the entire scene. 14 Figure 7: More qualitative results for movies. 15 Figure 8: More qualitative results for live videos.

sections.title: D EXPERIMENTAL SETTINGS
sections.content: Metrics. We evaluate identity transfer, target-attribute preservation, video quality, and inference efficiency. Following DreamID-V (Guo et al., 2026), we measure identity transfer using cosine similarity between ArcFace (Deng et al., 2019a) embeddings of the source image and generated frames, reported as ID Sim. We also annotate the displayed outputs with frame-level ID Sim. scores to facilitate comparison between embedding similarity and visual appearance. Following LivingSwap (Luo et al., 2026), we assess target-attribute preservation through distances between generated and corresponding target frames in estimated head pose (Pose) (Ruiz et al., 2018), expression coefficients (Expr.) (Deng et al., 2019b), and lighting coefficients (Light) (Deng et al., 2019b). Gaze preservation is measured by cosine similarity between their estimated 3D gaze vectors (Gaze) (Abdelrahman et al., 2023). We evaluate video quality using Frechet Video Distance (FVD). For efficiency, FPS measures the number of newly generated video frames output per second by the complete pipeline, excluding reused history frames. Latency measures the end-to-end time required for single in16 Figure 9: More qualitative results for AI-generated dramas. ference run. Both measurements include VAE encoding, denoising, VAE decoding, and output compositing. Implementation Details. We initialize our model from the pretrained DreamID-V checkpoint (Guo et al., 2026) and train Phase and Phase II for 1,000 iterations each. Both phases use learning rate of 105 and batch size of 8. In Phase II, each training rollout consists of five autoregressive generation windows. sections.title: E ABLATION OF TRAINING PHASE AND DENOISING STEPS
sections.content: Setup. We compare the DreamID-V initialization with 16 denoising steps, the Phase-I bidirectional model with 25 and 4 steps, and the final Phase-II streaming model with 4 steps. We evaluate identity similarity, target-attribute preservation, and end-to-end throughput to assess the effects of training phase and sampling budget. To contextualize the sampling results, we also track identity and attribute metrics along the denoising trajectories of DreamID-V and the Phase-I model. Results and interpretation. As shown in Table 3, the four-step Phase-I model improves identity similarity from 0.445 to 0.583 over the initialization and improves all four target-attribute metrics. Compared with 25-step sampling, it achieves comparable or slightly better identity, pose, expression, and lighting scores, together with higher gaze similarity, while increasing throughput from 6.702 to 30.280 FPS, 4.52 speedup. The final streaming model retains most of this identity similarity (0.577) and further improves pose, lighting, and gaze scores, with slight increase in expression error. Its throughput decreases to 21.174 FPS because streaming repeatedly processes overlapping history and incurs per-window overhead, while reused history frames are excluded from the output frame count. These results support four-step sampling as an efficient choice for rollout training and streaming inference. The trajectories in Fig. 10 provide further context for the sampling results. For our model, identity similarity improves through most of denoising before declining slightly near the endpoint, whereas expression and lighting errors generally increase after reaching their minima early in the trajectory. Thus, progressing further along the denoising trajectory does not consistently improve the evaluated 18 Figure 11: Joint Rec-ID supervision ablations on short200. (a) Weighting schedules. (b) Trade-offs across L1L7. (c) Threshold sweep for L2. Scores average direction-aligned, minmax-normalized identity and attribute metrics within each sweep. Blue lines connect Pareto-optimal configurations; stars mark the endpoint-distance knee points. Figure 12: Qualitative comparison of joint reconstructionidentity supervision schedules (L1L7). L2 balances source-identity transfer and target-attribute preservation. metrics. One possible explanation is that late-stage refinement introduces appearance details that do not necessarily improve identity or attribute similarity as measured by the evaluation encoders. This interpretation is consistent with the slightly better scores obtained with four-step sampling, although the trajectories alone do not establish why changing the step count produces these gains. Four-step sampling may still sacrifice some fine visual detail relative to 25 steps, so its favorable identity and attribute scores should not be interpreted as uniformly better perceptual quality. We compare seven piecewise-constant weighting configurations, L1L7, with the noise range divided at σ = 0.5 (Fig. 11(a)). The identity weight is either 0.1 or 0, and the reconstruction weight is either 10 or 0.1. For L2, we further vary the switching threshold τ over {0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7}, keeping the identity weight at 0.1 and the highand low-noise reconstruction weights at 10 and 0.1, respectively. We also compare clean-endpoint and velocity reconstruction under the L2 schedule and examine the gradient norms of the identity and two reconstruction losses during training. All configurations share the same initialization, training budget, and four-step evaluation protocol on the short200 benchmark of HumanFaceVid. Weighting configurations. L2 balances identity transfer and target-attribute preservation by retaining identity supervision throughout training while reducing the reconstruction weight at low noise levels. Compared with L1, it strengthens identity transfer with small changes in attribute preservation and imaging quality. Removing identity supervision from either noise interval weakens identity transfer (L3/L4/L7), whereas weakening high-noise reconstruction compromises target fidelity despite stronger identity similarity (L5/L6). The qualitative results in Fig. 12 illustrate this trade-off, particularly the changes in expression and lighting under L5/L6. Together with its knee-point position in Fig. 11(b), these results support L2 as balanced choice. Switching threshold. Increasing τ narrows the noise interval receiving strong reconstruction supervision, favoring identity transfer over target-attribute preservation. Across the sweep, identity similarity increases alongside expression and lighting errors, while pose and gaze vary nonmonotonically. Under the normalized aggregation in Fig. 11(c), τ = 0.4 achieves the highest attribute score and τ = 0.7 the highest identity score. We use τ = 0.5, the knee point of this trade-off. Reconstruction objective. We compare clean-endpoint and velocity reconstruction while keeping the velocity-prediction architecture unchanged. The training gradient norms in Fig. 13 indicate that endpoint reconstruction maintains more consistent gradient scale relative to identity supervision across noise levels. Under the L2 schedule, endpoint reconstruction achieves higher identity similarity, lower expression and lighting errors, and slightly higher gaze similarity, at the cost of higher pose error  (Table 4)  . We therefore adopt endpoint reconstruction for its favorable balance between identity transfer and target-attribute preservation.

sections.title: G ABLATION OF STREAMING WINDOW SIZE
sections.content: Setup. We vary the history length Nctx and generation length Ngen to examine the qualityefficiency trade-off in streaming inference. Following Sec. 4.3, each continuation generates Ngen new latent 20 Figure 14: More qualitative results for method comparisons on short video bench. frames conditioned on Nctx clean composited history frames, using bidirectional attention within the window. Unlike the main results, which use model trained with fixed (Nctx, Ngen) = (3, 9) configuration, this ablation uses model trained for 1,000 iterations with randomly sampled window sizes. Table 5 compares six configurations in terms of identity similarity, target-attribute preservation, and end-to-end throughput and latency. Increasing Ngen at fixed history length improves throughput but increases latency, Results. whereas increasing Nctx at fixed generation length adds computational overhead and reduces throughput. Among the evaluated configurations, (Nctx, Ngen) = (3, 9) achieves the highest FPS with lower latency than the larger-window alternatives. Target-attribute preservation generally improves with larger windows, while identity similarity peaks at (3, 3) and then declines. We therefore adopt (3, 9) as practical balance between throughput and latency, while maintaining competitive identity transfer and target-attribute preservation.
